name: Mooré
confidence_why: Compaoré's 2017 instrumental study of Ouagadougou Mooré finds lexical tone (H/L with downstep) and no detectable word accent, in line with the tone-language descriptions of Lehr, Redden & Balima 1966 and Nikiema 1975, and the only claims of a word accent are Rattray's 1918 pre-tonal sketch of Ghanaian Mōle (first syllable in disyllables, penultimate in longer words) and Houis 1960 as reported by Nikiema 1975 (root-syllable prominence with lengthening), which Nikiema reanalyses as morphological vowel length.
catalog_citation: Compaoré, Laetitia. 2017. Essai d'analyse de la prosodie du Mooré: ton et intonation. Thèse de doctorat, Université Paris Diderot / Université Sorbonne Paris Cité (NNT 2017USPCC170), 212 pp. HAL tel-02087494 (https://theses.hal.science/tel-02087494).

Typology (tone vs word-accent languages): ch. 1, pp. 16-17. Tone: ch. 4 'Présentation du mooré', pp. 54-57. Dialect: p. 52.
catalog_quote: En effet la définition du mot prosodique, repose sur l'accentuation de certaines syllabes. Or, mes corpus ne m'ont pas permis de détecter la présence d'une accentuation en mooré. Ainsi le mot prosodique tel que défini par Martin, ne peux pas être déterminé en mooré. [p. 128] ... Dans la théorie de Martin (1982), le regroupement prosodique dans les langues romanes se fait à partir des syllabes accentuées; or je n'ai pas été en mesure d'identifier une accentuation en mooré. J'ai simplement considéré que l'unité prosodique en mooré se regroupe autour d'un mouvement intonatif commun. [p. 186] ... Il est clair que le regroupement ne se fait pas autour de syllabes accentuées comme dans les langues romanes. [p. 188]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Mossi/Mooré (moss1236) is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title were read in full. (1) Compaoré 2017 (HAL thesis, held by the project) is a tone-and-intonation study that states twice, first-hand (pp. 128, 186), that no accentuation could be detected in Mooré; Mooré is a punctual-tone language (p. 55). This is the best statement found. (2) Auer & Uhmann 1988 (ZfS 7: 214-259, CC BY-NC-ND; full PDF downloaded from the the Internet Archive because the live De Gruyter site is WAF-could not be reached by automated download; saved to is a German survey of the stress-timing/syllable-timing debate that never mentions Mooré — the Glottolog link is spurious; not relevant. Three earlier-downloaded sources held by the project were re-read for context: Rattray 1918:14 (Ghanaian Mōle: accent on first syllable of disyllables, penult of longer words; pre-tonal), Houis 1960:52 as quoted in Nikiema 1975:57 (root syllables accented, cued by vowel length; Nikiema doubts the stress account and says stress, if pertinent, would be on the first syllable), and Lehr et al. 1966: xxxiv (tone language; loanword stress reinterpreted as high tone). Recommended coding if the language is added: tone language, no word stress identified (Compaoré 2017), with Rattray/Houis as older impressionistic root-initial/penult claims. Nothing left to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title's list; the earlier reading's unobtained print items (Canu 1973/1976, Kaboré 1985, Froger 1910, Peterson 1971, Kinda 1983, Houis 1960 original) remain the only potential further statements, all likely to repeat the tone-language picture. updated with the Auer & Uhmann line.

new_statements.quote: En effet la définition du mot prosodique, repose sur l'accentuation de certaines syllabes. Or, mes corpus ne m'ont pas permis de détecter la présence d'une accentuation en mooré. Ainsi le mot prosodique tel que défini par Martin, ne peux pas être déterminé en mooré. [p. 128] … Dans la théorie de Martin (1982), le regroupement prosodique dans les langues romanes se fait à partir des syllabes accentuées ; or je n'ai pas été en mesure d'identifier une accentuation en mooré. new_statements.translation: Indeed the definition of the prosodic word rests on the accentuation of certain syllables. But my corpora did not allow me to detect the presence of any accentuation in Mooré. Thus the prosodic word as defined by Martin cannot be determined in Mooré. [p. 128] … In Martin's (1982) theory, prosodic grouping in the Romance languages is built from the stressed syllables; but I was not able to identify any accentuation in Mooré. [p. 186]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mooré is a two-tone terraced-level tone language (H, L, with downdrift and downstep; tone-bearing unit = syllable; every syllable carries a tone). In an instrumental study of read and spontaneous speech (F0, duration, pauses), no word-level accentuation/stress could be detected; prosodic grouping is carried by F0 declination, F0 resetting, pauses and final-syllable lengthening at unit boundaries, not by stressed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Compaoré. Contradicting older claims, quoted in other opened sources: Rattray 1918:14 (Gold-Coast 'Mōle'): 'As a general rule in disyllables the accent is on the first syllable, in words of more than two syllables on the penultimate syllable'; Houis 1960:52 as quoted in Nikiema 1975:57: root syllables are 'accentuées par rapport aux syllabes non radicales', the accent marked by vowel lengthening — Nikiema rejects the lengthening-by-stress account (length is morphological) but writes 'Stress, if pertinent, would fall on the first syllable in both words'. Lehr, Redden & Balima 1966:xxxiii: stressed initial syllables of French/English loans are reinterpreted as Mooré high tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Compaoré's negative finding concerns accentuation within prosodic units of read sentences and spontaneous speech (utterance level, Ouagadougou dialect, instrumental); she states that the boundary lengthening she finds marks prosodic-unit edges, not word stress. Her ch. 4 phonology sketch (pp. 52-68) describes tone only and contains no accent statement. Rattray's and Houis's claims are about the word (root = first syllable of the CV-root + suffix word).
new_statements.identity_note: Compaoré 2017 describes the Ouagadougou (central, 'standard') dialect of Mooré, the author's own variety; Glottolog moss1236. Rattray 1918 describes 'Mōle', the Mooré of Mossi settlers in the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast (Ghana), an older and geographically peripheral variety; Nikiema 1975 is by a native speaker (dialect not stated) and quotes Houis 1960 on 'More' generally.

new_statements.translation: p.128: Indeed the definition of the prosodic word rests on the accentuation of certain syllables. But my corpora did not allow me to detect the presence of any accentuation in Mooré. Thus the prosodic word as defined by Martin cannot be determined in Mooré. p.186: ... but I was not able to identify an accentuation in Mooré. I simply took the prosodic unit in Mooré to be grouped around a common intonational movement.

new_statements.reading: First-hand, instrumental, native-speaker statement: Mooré (Ouagadougou dialect) is a lexical tone language (H/L, punctual tones, downstep/downdrift) in which no word-level stress/accent could be detected; prosodic phrasing is carried by F0 declination, not by accented syllables. The older claims of root-initial prominence (Houis 1960:52 via Nikiema 1975:57) and of first-syllable/penultimate accent (Rattray 1918:14, Ghanaian Mōle, pre-tonal description) are impressionistic and not confirmed by this study. If Mooré is added to the catalog, the defensible coding is 'tone language, no word stress reported' with Compaoré 2017 as the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: 20. Accent. — Il convient de se montrer circonspect dans la détermination de l’accent en mossi. [...] une certaine manière chantante dans le débit de la phrase mossi, due à ce que dans nos langues nous appelons le ton ou l’accent de hauteur, empêche de percevoir nettement l’accent d’intensité dans bien des mots. [...] Sans poser de principe absolu, on peut dire qu’en général l’accent d’intensité affecte la syllabe initiale du mot. Quant à la place de l’accent dans les mots composés et dans les monosyllabes, elle semble varier sous la double influence de l’apocope et du ton; il est préférable de ne proposer aucune hypothèse.
new_statements.translation: 20. Accent. — One must be cautious in determining the accent in Mossi. [...] a certain sing-song manner in the delivery of the Mossi sentence, due to what in our languages we call tone or pitch accent, prevents the intensity accent from being clearly perceived in many words. [...] Without laying down an absolute principle, one may say that in general the intensity accent falls on the initial syllable of the word. As for the place of the accent in compound words and in monosyllables, it seems to vary under the double influence of apocope and tone; it is preferable to propose no hypothesis.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (Compaoré 2017, instrumental, Ouagadougou dialect) codes Mooré as a tone language in which no word accentuation could be detected; Froger 1910 asserts a word-level intensity accent, generally on the initial syllable (type differs: initial stress vs. no stress). The contradiction is soft: Froger himself hedges ('sans poser de principe absolu'), reports that 'le ton ou l'accent de hauteur' masks the intensity accent in many words, and refuses a rule for compounds and monosyllables, i.e. a pre-tonal-analysis observer already noting pitch phenomena. His initial-accent claim lines up with the older impressionistic sources held by the project (Houis 1960:52 root-initial promine…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Impressionistic 1910 description (Ouagadougou-region Mossi): Froger posits an intensity (stress) accent that 'in general' falls on the word-initial syllable, stated explicitly without claiming an absolute rule; he warns that a sing-song delivery which he attributes to 'tone or pitch accent' often masks the intensity accent, that apocope can displace it, and he declines to state where it falls in compounds and monosyllables. The accent is the engine of his vowel phonology: post-tonic vowels weaken (apophonie, §§ 14-18) and drop (syncope, § 19), and ô is short whenever unaccented (§ 21). He marks the accent (acute) only where certain: on hiatus groups and before an apophonic vowel (pâôda, kwilïgha).
new_statements.exceptions: apocope displaces the accent (§ 20 n. 1, cf. §§ 37-44); place of accent in compound words and monosyllables left undetermined ('semble varier sous la double influence de l'apocope et du ton'); accent written only in hiatus groups and before an immediately following apophonic vowel; in three-vowel hiatus groups (dâôa) the accent is 'd'ordinaire' on the initial syllable (§ 18)
new_statements.identity_note: Froger 1910 describes the Mossi language (Mooré) of the 'boucle du Niger' (Ouagadougou region, then Haut-Sénégal-Niger); the catalog source Compaoré 2017 describes the Ouagadougou (central) dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Spencer, Juliann. 2010. Mòoré tonal polarity. Occasional Papers in Applied Linguistics (OPAL) 8 (ed. Steve Parker). Dallas: Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics [now Dallas International University].
tone_statements.quote: Mòòré is also a tone language. This means that each vowel in a word has a distinctive pitch, which can be high (H) or low (L). The H tone is indicated with the acute accent á, and the L tone with the grave accent à. Two words can be identical in shape but their meaning can vary if their tone melodies are different, as in the following examples: … HH báásé ‘dog’ …
tone_statements.locator: single-page poster, panel 1 'Representing the sounds of Mòòré', tone paragraph with the minimal pairs HH báásé 'dog' / HL báásè 'finish', LH zàgsé 'houses' / HL zágsè 'to water'
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, high and low; each vowel in a word bears a distinctive pitch; words identical in shape differ by tone melody (HH 'dog' vs HL 'finish', LH 'houses' vs HL 'to water'). Silent on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Kenstowicz, Michael J., Emmanuel Nikiema & Méterwa A. Ourso. 1988. Tonal polarity in two Gur languages. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 18(1): 77-103. Urbana: Department of Linguistics, University of Illinois.
tone_statements.quote: Crucial to our analysis is the postulation of an underlying three-way tonal contrast of high, low, and toneless stems. … Moore is a two-tone language of Buridna Faso. … In our transcriptions acute accent marks a high-toned syllable; low-toned syllables are unmarked. When a syllable has a long vowel, the tone is transcribed on the first half of the geminate. … Since hoore has the Itmttatton of one tone per syllable, the second of the two tones will always be realized on the number suffix (2b).
tone_statements.locator: p. 77 (abstract and sec. 1 'Some tonal rules of Moore') and p. 79 (first sentence)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, high and low, one tone per syllable; stems are underlyingly high, low or toneless and suffix tones are polar (high dissimilation); downdrift, and downstep from floating lows.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new conflict arises. The pre-existing tension recorded in the directory's remains: Compaoré 2017 (instrumental, Ouagadougou dialect) found no accentuation in Mooré, whereas Rattray 1918 p. 14 (Ghanaian Mōle, pre-tonal description) gives first-syllable accent in disyllables and penultimate in longer words, and Houis 1960:52 (via Nikiema 1975:57-58) reports root-syllable prominence marked by vowel lengthening, which Nikiema reanalyses as morphological length rather than stress. Froger 1910 could not be checked against any of these.

tone.says: P. 1 'The Mòoré language has two tonal levels: high and low (Kenstowicz 1994:390). Mòoré nouns show tonal polarity, as the tone of the number suffix is always the opposite of the tone of the root.' OT restatement: POLARITY ('Roots and suffixes have opposite tones') dominates H-SPREAD ('High tones spread to an adjacent low tone from left to right'); H spreading across a word boundary yields downstep (zá kór(downstep)gó 'bring a sack'). A 6-page student term paper re-analysing Kenstowicz, Nikiema…

sources.citation: Lehr, Marianne, James E. Redden & Adama Balima (1966). Moré basic course. Washington DC: Foreign Service Institute (ERIC ED012022).
sources.quote: "Whereas French and English words have characteristic stress in their original environments, they have characteristic pitch when transferred to a Moré utterance. The first syllable, of course, is the most important since it is interpreted to be the Moré stem syllable. Therefore, an initial stressed syllable is interpreted as high tone, and an initial weak syllable is interpreted as Moré low tone."
sources.locator: Introduction, section 'Tones of Borrowed Words', p. xxxiv (the page after the 'xxxiii' footer in the scanned)
sources.note: Pedagogical grammar treating Moré as a tone language (high/mid/low marking). Stress is mentioned only for loanwords: source-language stress on an initial syllable is reinterpreted as high tone on the stem syllable. No stress rule is given for native words.

sources.citation: Nikiema, Norbert (1975). Vowel length in Moore: its phonemic status and its orthographic representation. Proceedings of the Sixth Conference on African Linguistics, OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 20: 56-67. (quoting Houis, Maurice. 1960. Principes d'orthographe du More. Notes Africaines 86: 52)
sources.quote: "[Houis] suggested that such automatic lengthening could be attributed to the effects of stress ... a 'fonction de contraste' when 'les syllabes radicales sont accentuées par rapport aux syllabes non radicales et cette position sous l'accent est marquée par un allongement de la voyelle' (1960: 52). ... For example, length distinguishes meaning in (11) ba:ga 'dog' as opposed to baga 'diviner'. Stress, if pertinent, would fall on the first syllable in both words." [Houis: root syllables are accented relative to non-root syllables and this position under the accent is marked by vowel lengthening.]
sources.note: pp. 57-58: quotes Houis 1960:52 that root syllables are accented relative to non-root syllables and that the accent is marked by vowel lengthening; argues length is conditioned by a morpheme boundary + -C(V) suffix, not stress: 'Stress, if pertinent, would fall on the first syllable in both words … while stress may very well be necessary, it is not a sufficient condition for lengthening'.

sources.citation: Rattray, R. S. (1918). An elementary Mōle grammar, with a vocabulary of over 1000 words, for the use of officials in the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
sources.quote: "The Accent. As a general rule in disyllables the accent is on the first syllable, in words of more than two syllables on the penultimate syllable."
sources.note: Early colonial grammar of the Ghanaian (Northern Territories) variety, no tone marking: accent on the first syllable of disyllables, on the penult of longer words — i.e. penultimate. Impressionistic; later tonal descriptions (Lehr et al. 1966, Compaoré 2017) do not recognise word stress.

tone.says: P. 77 'Moore is a two-tone language of Bur[ki]na Faso. In this paper we build on some of the results in the excellent earlier tonal descriptions of Peterson (1971) and Kinda (1983).' Nouns show three surface patterns L-H, H-L, H-H and never L-L; analysis: roots are underlyingly H, L or toneless, the class/number suffix is H and dissimilates (H -> L / H __) after an H root, toneless roots get H from the suffix, so polarity is an epiphenomenon. p. 80: 'First, like many other African tonal languag…
